\begin{frontmatter}

\title{A high-order, matrix-free semi-Lagrangian level-set advection method
       for arbitrary polyhedral meshes}

\author[tud]{Tomislav Mari\'c}
\ead{maric@mma.tu-darmstadt.de}
\address[tud]{Mathematical Modeling and Analysis, Technische Universit\"at Darmstadt, Germany}

\begin{abstract}
We present a semi-Lagrangian (SL) advection scheme for the level-set equation that
is high order in space, free of any linear solve, and -- unlike most level-set
transport schemes -- runs unmodified on arbitrary polyhedral finite-volume meshes.
The level set is transported along characteristics, $\psilev^{\,n+1}(\xc)=\psilev^{\,n}(\xd)$,
with the departure foot $\xd$ obtained from a second-order Taylor backward step and
the field at the foot reconstructed by an inverse-distance-weighted quadratic
\emph{value} least-squares fit over a cell-neighbour stencil. Fitting field
\emph{values} (rather than injecting an independently computed gradient) is shown
to be the property that keeps the scheme stable up to Courant number one, where
gradient-injecting reconstructions diverge. The reconstruction stencil is chosen
per mesh: the point-neighbour (cell--point--cell) stencil on hexahedra, and the
compact face-neighbour (cell--face--cell) stencil on general polyhedra, where the
larger face valence already over-determines the quadratic fit. On a set of
reversible verification flows (a 2D vortex and the 3D shear and LeVeque deformation
fields) discretised on uniformly refined hexahedral and cfMesh polyhedral grids, the
geometric shape error converges at the \emph{same} order on structured and
unstructured meshes -- second to third order on the smooth flows and at the expected
reduced rate on the under-resolved deformation filament. A memory-lean, cache-free
implementation removes the large-$N$ memory ceiling at the cost of $\sim\!1.4\times$
the CPU of the cached variant, while producing bit-identical results. The method,
its runtime-selectable software design in OpenFOAM, and a fully reproducible
Snakemake study pipeline are described.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
level set \sep semi-Lagrangian \sep interface advection \sep polyhedral meshes \sep
least-squares reconstruction \sep OpenFOAM
\end{keyword}

\end{frontmatter}

% =============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
The level-set method represents an interface as the zero contour of a smooth
signed-distance field $\psilev$ and transports it by the linear advection equation
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial \psilev}{\partial t} + \uvec\cdot\nabla\psilev = 0 ,
  \label{eq:levelset}
\end{equation}
for a prescribed or coupled velocity $\uvec$~\cite{osher1988,sethian1999}. Its
appeal is a smooth field from which normals and curvature follow by
differentiation; its well-known costs are the loss of the signed-distance property
under advection (addressed by reinitialisation~\cite{sussman1994}) and the absence
of intrinsic volume conservation, which motivates geometric
volume-of-fluid alternatives on unstructured meshes~\cite{roenby2016,maric2020}.

Most level-set transport schemes are Eulerian and were developed on structured
Cartesian grids, where high-order upwind-biased flux reconstructions are
straightforward. On the unstructured, and in particular \emph{polyhedral}, meshes
used throughout industrial finite-volume practice the situation is markedly harder:
compact high-order stencils are irregular, and the geometric machinery that makes
Cartesian schemes cheap is unavailable. Semi-Lagrangian
methods~\cite{staniforth1991,strain1999}, which integrate the characteristic
equation backwards in time and reconstruct the field at the departure point, are an
attractive alternative because they avoid a flux integral and a linear solve
entirely. Their accuracy, however, hinges on the departure-point reconstruction,
and it is precisely this reconstruction that is delicate on general polyhedra.

This paper contributes a semi-Lagrangian level-set advection method that is
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep2pt
  \item \textbf{high order and CFL-robust} -- second to third order for the smooth
        flows up to Courant number one, obtained from a single weighted-least-squares
        quadratic fit of field \emph{values};
  \item \textbf{matrix-free} -- a per-cell assignment with one neighbour halo
        exchange, no assembled matrix and no linear solve;
  \item \textbf{mesh-agnostic} -- the same solver, with a mesh-appropriate stencil,
        converges at the same order on hexahedral and arbitrary polyhedral meshes;
  \item \textbf{reproducible} -- implemented with runtime model selection in
        OpenFOAM and driven by a Snakemake pipeline whose results feed both this
        article and the accompanying presentation from a single data source.
\end{enumerate}
We deliberately restrict the scope to \emph{advection}: reinitialisation and
mass-conservation corrections are orthogonal and are discussed as limitations
(Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).

% =============================================================================
\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Semi-Lagrangian update}
Equation~\eqref{eq:levelset} states that $\psilev$ is constant along
characteristics. The update is therefore the exact statement
\begin{equation}
  \psilev^{\,n+1}(\xc) = \psilev^{\,n}(\xd), \qquad
  \label{eq:sl}
\end{equation}
evaluated at every cell centre $\xc$: the arrival value equals the old-time value at
the foot $\xd$ of the characteristic through $\xc$. No flux, no divergence and no
linear system appear; the cost is one field reconstruction per cell.

\subsection{Second-order departure foot}
The foot is obtained by integrating $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\uvec$ backwards over one step
with a second-order Taylor expansion,
\begin{equation}
  \xd = \xc - \uvec^{\,n+1}\,\Delta t
        + \tfrac12\!\left[\frac{\uvec^{\,n+1}-\uvec^{\,n}}{\Delta t}
                 + \left(\uvec^{\,n+1}\!\cdot\nabla\right)\uvec^{\,n+1}\right]\!\Delta t^{2},
  \label{eq:foot}
\end{equation}
where $\nabla\uvec^{\,n+1}$ is a Gauss-linear cell gradient. The step is bounded by a
foot-radius guard: if $\lvert\xd-\xc\rvert$ exceeds the reconstruction stencil radius
the operational Courant limit ($\mathrm{CFL}\!\le\!1$) has been violated and the run
warns. This foot formula is held fixed throughout.

\subsection{Weighted least-squares value reconstruction}
\label{sec:recon}
The old-time field is reconstructed at $\xd$ by a per-cell quadratic fit over the
arrival cell's neighbour stencil $\mathcal{S}_c$. Writing
$\mathbf{d}_i=\mathbf{x}_i-\xc$ and fitting the increments $\psilev_i-\psilev_c$
against the quadratic basis $b_k(\mathbf{d})=\{d_x,d_y,d_z,\tfrac12 d_x^2,\dots,d_xd_y,\dots\}$
(nine terms in 3D, the constant dropped),
\begin{equation}
  R_c(\mathbf{x}) = \psilev_c + \sum_{k} a_k\, b_k(\mathbf{x}-\xc), \qquad
  \mathbf{a} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{a}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_c}
      w_i^{2}\bigl(R_c(\mathbf{x}_i)-\psilev_i\bigr)^2 ,
  \label{eq:wlsq}
\end{equation}
with inverse-distance weights $w_i=1/\lvert\mathbf{d}_i\rvert$. Because the constant
term is dropped, $R_c(\xc)=\psilev_c$ exactly, i.e.\ the reconstruction reproduces
the cell value. The normal equations are $5\times5$ (2D) or $9\times9$ (3D) and are
solved per cell; on a static mesh the (weighted) pseudo-inverse can be cached once so
that each step is a single matrix--vector product, or -- in the memory-lean variant
of Section~\ref{sec:software} -- recomputed by a Cholesky factorisation each step.

\paragraph{Why a value fit.}
A defining choice is that the reconstruction fits \emph{values}. Gradient-injecting
alternatives -- a Taylor expansion about $\xc$ using an independently computed cell
gradient, or a nested least-squares Hessian $\mathbf{H}=\nabla(\nabla\psilev)$ -- are
formally of the same order but were found to be unstable under semi-Lagrangian
feedback: the injected gradient is inconsistent with the reconstructed values, and
that inconsistency amplifies as the foot approaches the stencil edge near
$\mathrm{CFL}=1$, so $\gradpsi$ blows up. The single simultaneous value fit
in~\eqref{eq:wlsq} produces $\mathbf{a}$ (hence the gradient) as a \emph{by-product}
of a bounded projection, and remains second order at every Courant number.

\subsection{Mesh-adaptive stencil}
\label{sec:stencil}
The 3D quadratic fit~\eqref{eq:wlsq} needs at least nine independent neighbours. A
hexahedral cell has only six face neighbours, so on structured meshes the wider
\emph{cell--point--cell} (CPC) stencil -- the cell plus all cells sharing a vertex,
typically 26 neighbours -- is required. A cfMesh polyhedron, by contrast, has
$\sim$12--16 faces, so the compact \emph{cell--face--cell} (CFC) stencil already
over-determines the fit while being three to four times smaller, hence cheaper per
cell and better conditioned (it does not reach into the near-coplanar far field that
ill-conditions the sprawling point-neighbour fit). The stencil is therefore selected
per mesh -- CPC on hexahedra, CFC on polyhedra -- and this is the mesh-appropriate
default. The remote (processor/cyclic) neighbours are gathered through OpenFOAM's
extended-stencil \texttt{mapDistribute}, so a step needs exactly one halo exchange of
$\psilev^{\,n}$.

\subsection{Boundedness}
On irregular polyhedral stencils a near-singular local fit can produce large
coefficients; to keep the reconstruction bounded, the reconstructed value at the foot
is clamped to the range of $\psilev^{\,n}$ over the arrival stencil (a monotone clip).
The clamp is inactive in smooth regions -- where the foot value lies within the local
range for $\mathrm{CFL}\!\le\!1$ -- so it preserves the convergence order while
preventing the geometric runaway that an unbounded fit exhibits on distorted cells.

\subsection{Phase indicator}
The geometric error metrics below compare a phase indicator (volume fraction)
computed from $\psilev$ against the exact one. We use the analytic tetrahedral-fill
indicator of Detrixhe and Aslam~\cite{detrixhe2016}: the narrow-band cell is
decomposed into tetrahedra and each is filled analytically from the signed-distance
plane reconstructed by a local linear least squares, avoiding polygon-clipping
tolerances. The indicator is a diagnostic; it does not enter the advection.

% =============================================================================
\section{Software design and reproducibility}
\label{sec:software}
The method is implemented in OpenFOAM as the application
\texttt{leiaSemiLagrangeLevelSetFoam}. The reconstruction is a runtime-selectable
class hierarchy (\texttt{slReconstruction}): the production
\texttt{quadraticWeightedLeastSquares} fit and its cache-free twin
\texttt{uncachedQuadraticWeightedLeastSquares} are chosen from a dictionary, so a new
reconstruction is added without touching existing code. The two implementations are
identical up to floating-point association (verified cell-for-cell); the cache-free
variant assembles and Cholesky-solves the small normal equations every step, trading
$\sim\!1.4\times$ the CPU of the cached matrix--vector product for $\sim\!37\%$ less
memory and no large-$N$ ceiling. All verification studies are generated by a Snakemake
pipeline that materialises the cases, runs the solver, aggregates the error norms, and
emits the figures and CSV tables of this article into a single per-theme
\texttt{data/} folder; the article and the accompanying reveal.js presentation consume
that same folder, so both always reflect the newest results.

% =============================================================================
\section{Verification}
\label{sec:verification}

\subsection{Setup}
Three reversible benchmark flows are used. The 2D reversed single vortex and the 3D
shear and LeVeque deformation fields~\cite{leveque1996,rider1998} carry a sphere
(circle) out and, through a cosine-in-time reversal at $t=T$, back to its initial
position, so the exact solution at $t=T$ equals the initial condition and the
reversed error is a true accuracy measure without a closed-form mid-flow. Each flow is
run on a uniform refinement ladder chosen so that the cell count roughly doubles
($\sqrt2$ per direction in 2D) or quadruples ($\sqrt[3]{4}$ per direction in 3D) per
level, keeping the refinement ratio uniform for a clean order estimate while remaining
memory-manageable. The 3D cases are run on hexahedral (\texttt{blockMesh}) and
polyhedral (cfMesh~\cite{juretic_cfmesh}) grids at matching characteristic size
$h=1/N$. Errors are the volume-weighted $\Lp{2}$ gradient error
$\bigl\|\gradpsi-1\bigr\|$, the geometric shape error (indicator symmetric difference)
and the relative volume-conservation error, all measured at the reversed time $t=T$.
Convergence orders are least-squares slopes of $\log(\text{error})$ versus $\log h$.

\subsection{Two-dimensional convergence}
Figure~\ref{fig:conv2d} reports the 2D reversed vortex on the $\sqrt2$ ladder
($N=32\!\to\!256$) with \texttt{quadraticWeightedLeastSquares}. The geometric shape
and volume-conservation errors converge at close to third order and, decisively, the
order is essentially independent of the Courant number: shape order $2.97$ at
$\mathrm{CFL}=\tfrac12$ and $2.59$ at $\mathrm{CFL}=1$ (Table~\ref{tab:orders}). The
$\bigl\|\gradpsi-1\bigr\|$ order of $\approx0.5$ reflects the absence of
reinitialisation, not the transport accuracy.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.86\linewidth]{sl_2Dvortex_convergence.png}
  \caption{2D reversed vortex, $T=2$: gradient, geometric shape and
  volume-conservation error versus $h$ at $\mathrm{CFL}=\tfrac12$ and $1$ on the
  $\sqrt2$ refinement ladder. Shape and volume errors converge at $\approx O(h^{3})$,
  independent of the Courant number.}
  \label{fig:conv2d}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Three-dimensional convergence, hexahedral and polyhedral}
Figures~\ref{fig:conv3dshear} and~\ref{fig:conv3ddef} overlay the hexahedral and
polyhedral convergence for the 3D shear and deformation flows on the $\sqrt[3]{4}$
ladder; Table~\ref{tab:orders} collects the measured orders. On the filament-free
shear flow the hexahedral shape error converges at order $2.50$ (volume $\approx
O(h^{3})$), carrying the 2D second-order result into 3D. The LeVeque deformation is
the most demanding case: the sphere is drawn into a thin filament at $t=T/2$ that is
under-resolved on the grids reachable here, so the shape error converges at the
reduced rate of $\approx1.4$. Crucially, the \emph{hexahedral and polyhedral orders
agree} -- deformation shape order $1.36$ (hex, five levels) versus $1.46$ (poly, four
levels) -- so the convergence behaviour is mesh-agnostic even on the hard case. The
polyhedral shear run is a two-level spot-check (finer polyhedral shear grids exceeded
the memory of the test machine) whose errors are of comparable magnitude to the
hexahedral ones; the reliable hex$\leftrightarrow$poly comparison is the four/five
level deformation case.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.98\linewidth]{sl_3Dshear_convergence.png}
  \caption{3D shear, $T=3$, \texttt{quadraticWeightedLeastSquares}, $\mathrm{CFL}=\tfrac12$:
  hexahedral (solid) and polyhedral (dashed) convergence of the gradient, shape and
  volume error versus $h$.}
  \label{fig:conv3dshear}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.98\linewidth]{sl_3Ddeformation_convergence.png}
  \caption{3D LeVeque deformation (unit cube), $T=3$: hexahedral ($N=32\!\to\!160$) and
  polyhedral ($h=1/32\!\to\!1/128$) convergence. Hex and poly converge at the same
  (reduced, filament-limited) order; see Table~\ref{tab:orders}.}
  \label{fig:conv3ddef}
\end{figure}

  \caption{Least-squares convergence orders of the shape, volume and gradient error

  \label{tab:orders}

\subsection{Interface evolution}
Figures~\ref{fig:isoshear} and~\ref{fig:isodef} show the transported $\psilev=0$
iso-surface at $t=0$, $T/2$ and $T$ on the three finest grids of each 3D study,
rendered in a fixed orientation directly from the simulation fields. The initial
sphere (top), the strongly deformed interface at maximal deformation (middle), and the
recovered sphere at the reversed time (bottom) are visually consistent across
resolutions and mesh types, and the sharpening of the deformed interface with
refinement mirrors the measured convergence.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{isosurface_3Dshear_hex.png}
  \caption{$\psilev=0$ interface of the 3D shear flow (hexahedral) at $t=0$, $T/2$, $T$
  (rows) for the three finest resolutions (columns).}
  \label{fig:isoshear}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{isosurface_3Ddeformation_poly.png}
  \caption{$\psilev=0$ interface of the 3D LeVeque deformation on the \emph{polyhedral}
  mesh at $t=0$, $T/2$, $T$ (rows) for the three finest resolutions (columns): the same
  method on unstructured cells.}
  \label{fig:isodef}
\end{figure}

% =============================================================================
\section{Limitations and outlook}
\label{sec:limitations}
Three limitations define the scope. First, the scheme performs \emph{advection
only}: without reinitialisation the signed-distance property, and hence
$\gradpsi=1$, is not maintained over long integrations, which is why the
$\bigl\|\gradpsi-1\bigr\|$ order is low; a high-order redistancing partner is future
work. Second, as a level-set method it is not mass-conservative, unlike geometric
volume-of-fluid schemes on the same meshes~\cite{roenby2016,maric2020}; the volume
error is reported and converges, but conservation is not enforced. Third, the
foot must remain inside the reconstruction stencil, so the method is limited to
$\mathrm{CFL}\!\lesssim\!1$; its advantage there is high order at no linear-solve cost
and near-ideal parallel locality. Finally, we observed that the per-cell cost is
higher on polyhedra than on hexahedra because of the larger neighbour valence; the
compact face-neighbour stencil mitigates but does not eliminate this.

% =============================================================================
\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}
A matrix-free semi-Lagrangian level-set advection method has been presented that
attains second-to-third-order geometric accuracy up to Courant number one and, with a
mesh-appropriate least-squares stencil, converges at the same order on hexahedral and
arbitrary polyhedral finite-volume meshes. The key ingredient is an
inverse-distance-weighted quadratic reconstruction of field \emph{values} at the
departure foot, which -- unlike gradient-injecting reconstructions -- is stable under
semi-Lagrangian feedback. The method is realised with runtime model selection in
OpenFOAM and a fully reproducible study pipeline whose single data source drives both
this article and its companion presentation.
